"I was then a young and ambitious man, but I was also a man who
was not above a little gain. I began to find that I was making
much more money by my begging than by my writing. In fact, I
found that I was doing very well indeed. For years I followed
the two professions. I would dress at home in a cheap but

could make as much as 10 pounds and 12 pounds a week, and I was
fairly well to do. Then I met the lady who is now my wife, and
married her. I could not tell her of my way of living, and so I
was forced to lead a double life. For three years I was at my
old trade, but I was always afraid that someone who knew me
would see me and recognise me. For this reason I moved to Lee,
and used to leave my home every morning at the same hour as any
other City man, while really I was in town for only five or six

found, for I knew that the Lascar was to be trusted. It was
there that I kept my rags and my paints, and from there I
started out every morning for my station in Threadneedle Street.
This continued for years, and I was beginning to think that I was
safe until that fatal Monday. I was changing into my beggar's
clothes when I looked out of the window and saw my wife looking
directly at me. It was only by a great effort that I did not cry
out, and I believe I must have done so as she looked up. I drew
back, but she had seen me. I knew that in a few minutes she

had only time to throw my clothes into a corner, and to finish

"It is a most remarkable story," said Sherlock Holmes, with a

"The Lascar had agreed to post it for me. I gave him a gold piece

"And the pennies?"

"I had no other way of getting rid of them, and so I stuffed

"Yes," said Holmes, "it is a very interesting case. I think that

expensively, I should never have thought of such a career had I
not found it impossible to provide for my family by any other.

standing before me in the very midst of my masquerade. She saw me

there. Then I knew that my secret was out, and I turned into the
room, and I pulled off my clothes, and I threw them upon the bed,
and I got into my beggar's rags. My wife was at the door, but I
knew that she could not come into the room until she had been

that she came I should be a different man from the one she saw.
But I had no time. I had just finished my toilet when the door
burst open, and there she stood. She did not know me, but she saw
the clothes, and I think that if it had not been for the police,
she would have seen through my disguise. For my coat was missing,
and I had to hide it where I could. But for the rest you know. I

"By degrees I became richer and richer, and it was then that I
first thought of an occupation which should be more likely to
meet with the approval of my family. I had already a considerable
sum of money, which I had invested in house-property, and in
three years I was a comparatively wealthy man. It was then that I
married the daughter of a local brewer at Lee, after having
passed through many a trial of my self-control in order to keep
my secret. For I felt that my wife's love was the most precious
thing in my life, and that if she ever guessed that my wealth was
won in such a way, it would be the end of our happiness. So I
went on for several years, always leaving home as a man of
business and returning as one. My children never dreamed that
their father, whom they saw in his carriage on Sundays, was the
same man who sat as a beggar in Threadneedle Street. I began to
believe that I should die with the secret, but a chance
combination of circumstances has at last revealed it."

"And that was your wife's visit to the City?" said Holmes.

"Well, I was a wealthy man. I had a wife and children, and
everything that heart could wish. One day my wife would come into
town, and I would be back in my home at Lee, but the money must
continue to flow. I never told her a word, and my life was one of
complete success.

"On Monday morning, however, I went into town to see my agent,
had a little breakfast, and then went to the room in Swandam Lane
to change into my beggar's dress. I had just taken off my coat
and had not yet painted my face when I heard a cry of horror from
the street, and looking out, I saw my wife standing upon the
pavement and looking up at me. I was paralyzed with fear, but I
remember waving my hands to her as though I would warn her off.
The next moment she had disappeared from my sight and I was alone
in the room. I knew that she would be at the door in a few
minutes, so I hurriedly took off my remaining clothes and hid
them in a drawer. I had just time to don my beggar's dress when I
heard her voice on the stairs, and I had only just had time to
throw the window up when she burst into the room. I was so
overwhelmed with shame and fear that I was on the point of
confessing all when she fainted. I could then think of nothing
but how I could get her away before she recovered her senses and
should recognize me. I knew that she would be back with the
police, and I was in such a state of terror that I did not know

"And the bloodstains?" asked Holmes.

"They were from a cut in my finger which I had made in my
excitement," said the prisoner.

"And the letter?"

"I gave it to the Lascar and told him to post it in Gravesend,
where he had friends."

"I see it all now," said Holmes, with a smile. "And a very pretty
little problem it was, too."

"As I grew richer I grew more ambitious, took a house in the
country, and eventually married, without anyone having a
suspicion as to my real occupation. My dear wife knew that I had
business in the City. She little knew what.

"It is a most remarkable narrative," Sherlock Holmes remarked, "and it confirms the few links which were missing from my own chain of reasoning. You see, Watson, the weighted coat and the disappearance of the gentleman were all parts of a desperate mask. Inspector, I trust that in the absence of a victim, the charge of murder must necessarily be dropped. There remains, perhaps, a minor charge of vagrancy, but surely the interests of justice would not be served by ruining a reputation and breaking a lady's heart over a matter that has already been so painfully resolved." Bradstreet nodded slowly, tapping his chin with his pencil. He agreed that provided Mr. St. Clair made a full confession of his activities to the Chief Commissioner, and solemnly swore to abandon his career in Threadneedle Street forever, the police would be satisfied to let the "Man with the Twisted Lip" vanish into the shadows from which he had emerged.

"Well, Mr. St. Clair," said Inspector Bradstreet, "I have heard many strange things in my time, but this certainly tops them all. You have led us a pretty dance, and I am not sure that I should not have you charged with obstructing the police. However, if no charge of murder can be brought against you, I suppose there is no reason why you should be detained. But I must insist that the beggar Hugh Boone disappears from the City from this day forward. If he is ever seen again, everything must come out."

"I have no more to say," he ended, his head sinking upon his
breast. "I have told you the naked truth, however much it may
shame me. I have lived two lives, and the one has at last
overtaken the other. You have my secret, and with it you have the
power to blast my name and to bring sorrow to my hearth. I can
only hope that, as no legal crime has been committed, you may
find it in your hearts to exercise a discretion which will save a
family from a blow which they have done nothing to deserve."

"I do not know that there is much more to be said," observed Inspector Bradstreet, closing his notebook with a sharp snap. "The case is certainly one of the most extraordinary in the annals of Bow Street, but as no crime has been committed, I see no reason why the law should interfere further. However, Mr. St. Clair, you must understand that this masquerade must end here and now. If Hugh Boone is ever seen again in the streets of London, the authorities will have no choice but to make the entire matter public. For the sake of your family's reputation and your children’s future, I trust that this lesson has been sufficiently severe and that you will find a more conventional method of providing for your household."

"I have little more to add," he said, with a weary gesture of his hands. "I have lived a lie for so long that the truth feels like a strange language. My only motive was to provide a life of comfort for my family, a life that my modest salary as a journalist could never have secured. I have played the part of Hugh Boone with such success that I became him in the eyes of the City, yet I remained Neville St. Clair in the heart of my home. It was a desperate game, and I have lost. I ask for no pity for myself, but I implore you to consider the children. If this scandal becomes public, their lives will be blighted by the shadow of my deception. I have made my confession; let the law do with me what it will, provided my secret remains within these walls."

"I do not know that there is anything else for me to explain. I
was determined to preserve my disguise as long as possible, and
hence my preference for a dirty face. Knowing that my wife would
be terribly anxious, I slipped off my ring and confided it to the
Lascar at a moment when no constable was watching me, together
with a hurried scrawl, telling her that she had no cause to
fear."

"That note only reached her yesterday," said Holmes.

"Good God! What a week she must have spent!"

With the promise of discretion from the inspector and a solemn vow from the prisoner, the strange case of the gentleman-beggar was brought to a quiet conclusion. Neville St. Clair was permitted to return to his home at the Cedars, where his relief was matched only by the joy of the wife who had never wavered in her faith. The public remained none the wiser, and the hideous figure of Hugh Boone vanished forever from the corners of Threadneedle Street, taking his secrets with him. As for Holmes, he remained silent during our journey back to Baker Street, save for a single observation on the remarkable lengths to which a man might go to secure a fortune for his family. It was a singular ending to a singular adventure, and one which I have often looked back upon as a testament to my friend's uncanny ability to see the truth behind even the most grotesque of masks.

"In that case," said Holmes, as he turned to leave the cell, "the mystery is at an end, and we may return to our more mundane duties. It has been a remarkable instance of how a man may lead two lives and yet remain himself, but I think, Watson, that the air of the country will be all the more pleasant for our having cleared this shadow from The Cedars. Let us hasten to the station, for I am sure that there is a lady in Kent who is waiting most impatiently for the news we bring."

"In that case, the secret is safe," said Holmes, as he rose and gathered his belongings. "Bradstreet, I am sure that we can rely upon your professional discretion. As for you, Mr. St. Clair, I trust that your future 'investments' will be of a nature that you need not hide from those who love you. Come, Watson, our work here is done. The morning air is sharp, and I find that the resolution of a mystery is an excellent stimulant for the appetite. Let us see what breakfast awaits us at Baker Street."

"In that case," said Holmes, "the problem may be regarded as settled. I think, Watson, that we shall be just in time for a late breakfast. If you will have the kindness to drive us to the station, Inspector, we shall be greatly obliged to you." And so, with a friendly nod to the official, we left the scene of this strange adventure, and as we rattled back towards London in the early morning light, I could not but marvel once again at the singular reasoning of my friend, which had unmasked the secret of Neville St. Clair and restored peace to his anxious household.

"In that case," said Bradstreet, "the matter may rest, but remember that the eye of the law is upon you. Mr. Holmes, we are all much indebted to you for your assistance in this strange affair." 

"I reached the conclusion," Holmes remarked as we walked toward the door, "by the simple process of elimination and a significant amount of tobacco. Come, Watson! I believe that if we hurry, we shall be back at Baker Street just in time for a very excellent breakfast."

"In that case I think that it is probable that no further steps
may be taken. But if you are found again, then all must come out.
I am sure, Mr. Holmes, that we are very much indebted to you for
having cleared the matter up. I wish I knew how you reach your
results."

"I reached this one," said my friend, "by sitting upon five
pillows and consuming an ounce of shag. I think, Watson, that if
we drive to Baker Street we shall just be in time for breakfast."
